q: Which subzone became the Languedoc's first named cru in 1999, and what distinguishes it from the appellation around it?
accept: minervois-la liviniere in 1999, limestone terraces below the montagne noire, syrah grenache mourvedre reds
la liviniere, first languedoc cru, red only with lower yields and longer ageing
minervois la liviniere on the petit causse, altitude and limestone, syrah-led blends
la liviniere elevated 1999 as the first cru of the minervois
ans: Minervois-La Livinière — six communes on the limestone terraces of the Petit Causse, on the south-facing foot of the Montagne Noire, above and behind the Minervois plain. Reds only, with Syrah, Grenache and Mourvèdre required to lead the blend, lower yields and longer compulsory ageing than Minervois itself, and the altitude and the mountain's shadow give freshness the plain cannot. The name is now often shortened to La Livinière.
exp: La Livinière set the template every later promotion followed — Corbières-Boutenac in 2005, Terrasses du Larzac in 2014, Pic Saint-Loup in 2017. Note the contrast with Boutenac, which mandates Carignan: here the Syrah-Grenache-Mourvèdre trio leads and Carignan is limited. The Languedoc is building a cru ladder subzone by subzone, and the examiner wants the sequence, not just the name.

q: Name the Muscat vins doux naturels of the Languedoc, Roussillon and Corsica, say which Muscat each may use, and explain mutage.
accept: frontignan mireval lunel saint-jean-de-minervois and rivesaltes, muscat blanc a petits grains except rivesaltes which may add alexandria
muscat blanc a petits grains for all but rivesaltes, mutage is fortifying the fermenting must with neutral spirit
frontignan lunel mireval st jean de minervois rivesaltes cap corse, spirit added during fermentation to keep sugar
mutage adds grape spirit mid-ferment, up to 10 percent of volume, leaving 100 grams of sugar
ans: In the Languedoc: Muscat de Frontignan, Muscat de Mireval, Muscat de Lunel and Muscat de Saint-Jean-de-Minervois, all 100% Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. In Roussillon: Muscat de Rivesaltes, the only one that may blend Petits Grains with Muscat of Alexandria. Corsica adds Muscat du Cap Corse, again Petits Grains. Mutage is the fortification step: neutral grape spirit of around 96% is run into the fermenting must, killing the yeast and leaving the grape's own sugar unfermented. The spirit must fall between 5% and 10% of the volume; the wines finish at roughly 15–18% alcohol with at least 100 g/l of residual sugar, and the best Muscats are bottled early and protectively to keep the grape aroma.
exp: Two distinctions win the point. First, vin doux naturel is fortified during fermentation (like Port) whereas vin de liqueur — Pineau des Charentes, Floc de Gascogne, Macvin — is fortified before it starts. Second, the Muscats are made reductively for freshness while the Grenache-based VDN of Banyuls, Maury and Rivesaltes are the oxidative, rancio side of the same law. A candidate who adds Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is correct — same VDN law, same Petits Grains, but in the southern Rhône rather than the Midi. The technique is credited to Arnau de Vilanova at Montpellier in the thirteenth century.

q: Why does Domaine de Trévallon, one of southern France's most famous reds, sell under an IGP?
accept: les baux capped cabernet sauvignon so trevallon declassified to igp alpilles
the wine is half cabernet sauvignon, more than les baux allows, so it labels as igp
durrbach refused to change the blend when les baux limited cabernet, now igp alpilles
cabernet sauvignon exceeds the appellation limit, sold as igp alpilles bouches-du-rhone
ans: Trévallon lies in Les Baux-de-Provence but is roughly half Cabernet Sauvignon, half Syrah. When the Les Baux appellation rules were finalised, Cabernet Sauvignon was capped at a small share of the blend — around 20% — and Éloi Dürrbach chose to declassify rather than alter a wine he had built over twenty years. It has been sold ever since as IGP Alpilles, formerly Vin de Pays des Bouches-du-Rhône, from vines on the limestone scree of the Alpilles.
exp: The lesson is the same one Mas de Daumas Gassac and Sassicaia teach: the tier on the label reports conformity with a rulebook, never quality, and in France's south the most ambitious wines have repeatedly been the ones outside the appellation. It is worth adding that Les Baux is among France's most thoroughly organic and biodynamic appellations, so the split was over grape variety alone, not philosophy.

q: Jurançon makes a great sweet wine without botrytis. Explain how, and what Petit Manseng contributes.
accept: passerillage on the vine in the dry fohn wind, late picking in tries, petit manseng thick skins and high acid
grapes raisin on the vine rather than rotting, petit manseng concentrates sugar and keeps acidity
late harvest passerillage into december, petit manseng for moelleux and gros manseng for sec
no botrytis, the wind dries the berries; petit manseng small thick-skinned berries hold acid
ans: Jurançon's sweetness comes from passerillage — grapes left hanging into late autumn and picked in successive tries through November and sometimes December, shrivelling on the vine in the warm dry föhn wind coming off the Pyrenees while cold nights preserve acidity. Botrytis is neither wanted nor reliable here. Petit Manseng is the grape that makes it work: small, thick-skinned, loose-clustered berries that resist rot and dehydrate rather than rotting, concentrating sugar while holding ferocious acidity. Gros Manseng, larger-berried and less concentrated, does most of the work in Jurançon Sec. The result is candied citrus, mango, ginger and spice, cut by an acidity that keeps it from cloying — 'moelleux' for the sweet wines, with Vendanges Tardives at the top.
exp: There are three routes to concentrated sugar and a candidate should be able to name all three and place this one: noble rot (Sauternes, Tokaji, the Neusiedlersee), freezing (Eiswein), and raisining on the vine or on mats (Jurançon, Vin de Paille, Amarone). Sauternes sits on the same latitude but depends on the Ciron's autumn mists; Jurançon's mountain wind does the opposite job, drying the fruit rather than damping it.

q: Explain the 'Rioja Alta vs Alavesa vs Oriental' triad in soils and style.

alavesa limestone alta mixed oriental warm
ans: Alta: clay-limestone/ferrous, structured; Alavesa: calcareous, higher, perfumed; Oriental (ex-Baja): warm, alluvial, Garnacha's home

q: Name the founding Rioja bodegas that imported Bordeaux technique in the 19th century, and explain the French connection.
accept: marques de riscal murrieta cvne lopez de heredia
ans: Marqués de Murrieta (1852) and Marqués de Riscal (1858), both founded by Spanish aristocrats who studied or lived in Bordeaux — Riscal hired the Bordeaux-trained Jean Pineau via the Diputación de Álava — followed by López de Heredia (1877) and CVNE (1879). The French link is technique, not migration: oïdium and later phylloxera drove French négociants into Rioja from the 1860s–80s as buyers, entrenching barrique aging.
exp: American oak later became the house accent for economic reasons.
